rows.title: All the way around
rows.text: If you are a Canada goose, each of your eyes sees a field about 155 degrees wide off to its side. If you are a mallard, a Canada goose or a northern shoveler, your two eyes overlap in front of you over about 20 degrees. Nobody has measured how wide one eye's field is in most other ducks, so nobody can yet say how much of the way around you they cover.
rows.note: Left out the mallard single-eye field (R29): its quote is a bare table row that does not label the 183.

rows.title: Below the bill
rows.text: The tip of your bill sits at an angle that was measured by looking at light that comes back out of the eye. If you are a mallard, that angle is about 105 degrees. If you are a Canada goose, it is about 80 degrees, which is 25 degrees less than in a mallard.
rows.note: The records give only the angle and not what it is measured from, so I made no claim about what you see below the bill. The title may need a record that defines the angle.

rows.title: Geese differ
rows.text: If you are a Canada goose, the tip of your bill projects at about 80 degrees, the smallest angle measured in any of these geese and swans. If you are a pink-footed goose it is about 100 degrees, and if you are a brant it is about 115. Nobody has measured it in the mute swan, the greylag goose or several other geese and swans.
rows.note: Records give only the angle value, not its reference direction, so the row does not say what 80 degrees is measured from.

rows.title: Color
rows.text: If you are a mallard, a table in a review of earlier measurements lists a violet-sensitive cone in your eye. Nobody has measured how many kinds of color-sensing cell you have. In the Nēnē, a Hawaiian goose, a study found a violet-sensitive cone as well, so a violet-sensitive cone may be common among ducks and geese, though for most of them nobody has measured it.
rows.note: Replaced "reports" and dropped the nanometer figures because they had no comparison to do. R1's other columns are unlabeled and R2's value is cut off, so I left out the other cone peaks and the cone count.

rows.title: Sharpness
rows.text: A human reads about 30 cycles a degree on an eye chart, and a compilation of bird eyes lists about 12 for the mallard, estimated from how densely nerve cells are packed in its retina. If you are a mallard, you see about two fifths of the fine detail a human sees, and if you are a Canada goose, about a third. The same compilation gives about 11 for the lesser scaup, the greater scaup and the northern shoveler.
rows.note: Figures are anatomical estimates from a compilation (Caves 2024). Other ducks are not measured or are only carried from relatives, so they are left out.

rows.title: Speed
rows.text: Nobody has measured how fast a flicker can flash before you stop seeing it as flicker. No record gives that figure for a duck, a goose or a swan, and a figure from another bird would not be yours. Humans stop seeing flicker at about 60 flashes a second, and nobody can yet say whether you see more or fewer.
rows.note: No records were provided, so the row states only that the flicker limit is unmeasured; the human 60 flashes a second figure comes from the prompt.

rows.title: Touch
rows.text: A review describes very high numbers of touch-sensing units in the bill-tip organ of filter-feeding and dabbling ducks, so if you feed that way, the tip of your bill very likely holds many of them. Nobody has measured how sensitive the rest of your body is to touch.
rows.note: R1 covers only filter-feeding and dabbling ducks, so geese, swans and other ducks get no claim. No record gives touch measurements for the rest of the body. Removed "reports" per the voice check.
